title: Like many others, this BERA article wasn't peer reviewed
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Vainker continues his campaign against low-quality educational research by dissecting a recent BERA journal paper, a systematic review of generative AI in education, which he argues shows no sign of real peer review. He points to a theme-network figure whose labels are meaningless words, a fabricated quotation, and abstract claims the results do not support. The 73 percent student-use figure rests on a single study of 36 students, and a national-strategy claim rests on one Thai paper against none from the UK. A methods sentence borrowed from an unrelated study of Indian family businesses reveals, he says, the telltale slip of AI-generated prose. His conclusion is that BERA is not maintaining editorial standards and that other academics are too timid to say so.
points: Vainker treats the paper as evidence that BERA journals publish AI-generated work without adequate peer review.
Specific defects include a nonsense theme figure, a quotation that does not appear in the cited source, and abstract statistics absent from the results.
Large claims are built on tiny evidence: a 73 percent student AI-use figure traces to one study of 36 students.
A methods sentence lifted from a paper on ESG risks in Indian family businesses shows how AI blurs the fine distinctions scholarship depends on.
He argues that silence from other academics suggests educational journals are simply not being read critically.
quotes: But so many - almost all - of the papers are worthless, going into slick, tedious technical detail to say nothing of interest. And sometimes they are just utter garbage; completely useless to anyone.

It is these papers that have led me to believe that BERA is not following proper peer review. I have pointed to many examples before (I still don’t understand how an AI-written review of tax evasion research made it into a leading educational journal), but here’s one published last week.

There are various further problems, including a fake quotation - ‘blurred continuum between legitimate assistance and academic misconduct’ does not appear in the article cited. More seriously, the central claims in the abstract are not supported in the results.

It does not appear in the results section, but reappears in the discussion (and introduction, for some reason). It is also makes a wild claim of ‘differential national strategies shaped by educational traditions, regulatory frameworks and technological infrastructure’ based on… 1/8 Thai papers covering curriculum integration as opposed to 0/7 UK papers.

This paper is the kind of garbage that I am campaigning against - absolute slop, absolute nonsense. If BERA had maintained any kind of editorial standards this would have been flatly rejected. It is the lowest effort AI production that a cursory read would have discounted (it also provides endless page numbers for indirect citations).
